title: Emergency-contact primary-update race — root-cause confirmation and fix

priorF1004P1EvidenceFile.note: Only existed on unmerged/closed PR #311, which self-recorded supersession by PR #310.

rootCause.explanation: PR #310's optimistic-concurrency 'prior primary' snapshot was read via a separate, unlocked prisma.patientEmergencyContact.findFirst() call issued before prisma.$transaction() opened. That query and the transaction's own connection checkout compete independently for the same pg pool (server/src/db.ts, default max 10). Under contention, the losing request's prior-read could be delayed until after the winning request's entire transaction had already committed, causing the in-lock recheck to find no discrepancy.
rootCause.whyStressTestCouldPass: The failure is scheduling-sensitive: it requires the exact window between the decoupled pre-check read and the transaction's own connection checkout to straddle the competing request's full commit. Repeated back-to-back rounds on an otherwise-idle process do not reliably reproduce that specific contention pattern.

firstAttempt.failingAssertion: patientEmergencyContactsPrimaryConcurrency — CREATE-race stress, round 0: exactly one concurrent create must succeed — got A=201 B=201
firstAttempt.rootCauseTheory: when no primary contact exists yet for a patient, both the prior-read and current-read return null for whichever request runs second; if that request's entire DB interaction is scheduled strictly after the first request's full commit, its own current-read (post-lock-acquire) sees the first request's newly-committed row, not the null its own prior-read captured moments earlier — BUT when neither read observed a primary at all (both null), priorPrimary.id === currentPrimary.id (both undefined/null), so no conflict is thrown and the second request silently takes over. This is the residual limitation already documented in rootCause and fixSelected.residualLimitation above, empirically observed in real CI for the first time.

impossibilityAnalysis.claim: no purely database-side design (using only signals visible from inside the promoting transaction) can distinguish a request whose entire transaction genuinely executes after a competitor's commit from a request that arrived later with deliberate intent — the two produce byte-for-byte identical database states
